title: Arian Controversy

date.note: From Arius's teaching in Alexandria (c. 318, the Thalia) through the Council of Constantinople (381), which reaffirmed the Nicene faith. The endpoints are the standard scholarly range; the controversy itself had many phases and local settlements in between.

summary: (D) The Arian controversy (c. 318-381) was the dispute over whether the Son is eternal God of the Father's essence or a creature made out of nothing who 'once was not'. Arius taught the latter in his Thalia; Athanasius defended the former; the Council of Nicaea (325) condemned Arius, but the dispute continued for over fifty years until the Council of Constantinople (381) reaffirmed the Nicene faith. John 1:1 was the central text: both sides appealed to 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God', Arius reading 'beginning' as the Word's creation, Athanasius reading it as his eternity. (A) The verse itself states neither the Arian nor the Nicene formulation.
citation: Athanasius, Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse I, ch. 2, §§5-6 (Thalia fragments), NPNF2 vol. 4. New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28161.htm. For the 325-381 span: The Nicene Creed: 325 and 381, Nicaea I, Creed of AD 325, and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, received text, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 14 (1900), ed. Henry R. Percival. Texts checked at https://apostolicatlas.com/early-church/councils/nicene-creed/ (quoting the Percival translation) and https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/basis/nicea1.txt (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Documents from the First Council of Nicea, from the same Percival edition).
notes: The range 318-381 is the conventional span for the controversy as a whole, not the duration of any single dispute or council. Intermediate phases (e.g. the councils of the 350s, the exile of Athanasius and Hilary) are not separately recorded here.

title: Council of Nicaea

date.note: The council met at Nicaea in 325, convened by Constantine to settle the Arian dispute; the year is given in the title of the NPNF2 vol. 14 documents checked.

summary: (D) The Council of Nicaea (325) condemned Arius and set forth a creed confessing the Son as 'the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father', and anathematised all who say 'there was a time when the Son of God was not', or that he was made of things that were not, or is a creature. The council's use of 'of one substance' (homoousios) turned on John 1:1 and the question whether the Word 'was God' eternally or was made. (A) John 1:1 itself does not use the word homoousios; the council's term is a later formulation (D) applied to the text, not a statement of the text.
citation: The Nicene Creed: 325 and 381, Nicaea I, Creed of AD 325, and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, received text, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 14 (1900), ed. Henry R. Percival. Texts checked at https://apostolicatlas.com/early-church/councils/nicene-creed/ (quoting the Percival translation) and https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/basis/nicea1.txt (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Documents from the First Council of Nicea, from the same Percival edition).
notes: Athanasius, present at Nicaea as a deacon, is listed as an author involved; he did not author the creed. Arius is listed as the writer whose teaching was condemned. The Nicene Creed is also recorded as a separate creed milestone (nicene-creed-325).

title: Nicene Creed (325)

date.note: Set forth by the Synod at Nicaea, 325, as stated in the NPNF2 vol. 14 text checked.

summary: (D) The Nicene Creed of 325 confesses 'one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father. By whom all things were made.' It ends with the brief clause 'And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost', followed by anathemas against those who say there was a time when the Son was not. The creed's Son language turns on John 1:1 ('the Word was God', 'all things were made by him'); (A) the verse itself does not state the creed's terms.
citation: The Nicene Creed: 325 and 381, Nicaea I, Creed of AD 325, and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, received text, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 14 (1900), ed. Henry R. Percival. Texts checked at https://apostolicatlas.com/early-church/councils/nicene-creed/ (quoting the Percival translation) and https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/basis/nicea1.txt (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Documents from the First Council of Nicea, from the same Percival edition).
notes: Recorded as a separate creed milestone because its text was verified distinctly from the council's other acts. No single author is named for the creed.

title: Council of Constantinople

date.note: The council met at Constantinople in 381 under Theodosius the Great; the year is given in the NPNF2 vol. 14 material checked.

summary: (D) The Council of Constantinople (381) reaffirmed the Nicene faith and is associated with the received form of the creed that expands the confession of the Holy Spirit: 'the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spake by the prophets.' The Spirit clause turns on John 15:26 ('the Spirit of truth which proceedeth from the Father'), the text Gregory of Nazianzus had expounded in his Fifth Theological Oration (380). (A) John 15:26 itself states that the Spirit proceeds from the Father; it does not state the creed's worship clause. Gregory of Nazianzus led the council during part of its sessions; he is not the author of the creed.
citation: The Nicene Creed: 325 and 381, Nicaea I, Creed of AD 325, and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, received text, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 14 (1900), ed. Henry R. Percival. Texts checked at https://apostolicatlas.com/early-church/councils/nicene-creed/ (quoting the Percival translation) and https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/basis/nicea1.txt (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Documents from the First Council of Nicea, from the same Percival edition).
notes: FLAG: the received 381 creed text's exact relation to the 381 meeting is debated (the checked source notes its compositional history and connection with the council's proceedings are discussed in scholarship, and Chalcedon's acts in 451 are an important witness to the received attribution). The milestone is therefore recorded with a partially-verified record, not verified. The Constantinopolitan Creed is also recorded as a separate creed milestone (constantinopolitan-creed-381).

title: Constantinopolitan Creed (Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed)

date.note: Received form associated with AD 381; its exact relation to the 381 council's proceedings is debated (see notes).

summary: (D) The received form associated with 381 confesses 'one Lord Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father before all worlds, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made', and adds the expanded Spirit clause: 'And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spake by the prophets.' The Spirit clause turns on John 15:26. (A) The verse itself does not state the worship clause or the creed's full form.
citation: The Nicene Creed: 325 and 381, Nicaea I, Creed of AD 325, and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, received text, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 14 (1900), ed. Henry R. Percival. Texts checked at https://apostolicatlas.com/early-church/councils/nicene-creed/ (quoting the Percival translation) and https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/basis/nicea1.txt (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Documents from the First Council of Nicea, from the same Percival edition).
notes: FLAG: the checked source states that the received 381 text's sources, its exact relation to that council's proceedings, and its connection with other fourth-century creedal forms are debated, and that the two texts (325 and 381) should not be treated as if an editor merely added one line in 381. Recorded as partially-verified.

title: Third Council of Toledo (589) — Filioque in the Creed

date.note: Third Council of Toledo met in 589; Schaff (citing Hefele, Hist. of the Councils, vol. IV, p. 416) records that in 589 the newly converted Goths were required to sign the creed with the Filioque addition, and that 589 is the earliest date at which the words are found introduced into the Creed.

summary: The Third Council of Toledo (589), at which the Visigothic kingdom under King Reccared renounced Arianism, is the earliest council at which the words 'and the Son' (Filioque) are found introduced into the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed: the newly converted Goths were required to sign the creed with the addition, so that the Spirit is confessed as proceeding from the Father 'and the Son'. (D) This is a later Western formulation about the Spirit's procession, not a statement of any biblical text; the council itself appears to have believed it was reciting the unaltered creed of Constantinople. The addition later became a central point of East-West dispute. Rome did not adopt the addition until 1014 (Benedict VIII, at the request of Henry II); Leo III had opposed the insertion (809).
citation: Philip Schaff, ed., Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, vol. 14, Historical Excursus on the Introduction into the Creed of the Words 'and the Son', Christian Classics Ethereal Library, https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf214/npnf214.ix.iv.html (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Philip Schaff, ed., A Select Library of Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers of the Christian Church, Second Series, vol. 14: The Seven Ecumenical Councils (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1900). Corroborated by: Henry R. Percival (ed.), 'Historical Excursus on the Introduction into the Creed of the Words "and the Son"', in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 14 (The Seven Ecumenical Councils). https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nicene_and_Post-Nicene_Fathers:_Series_II/Volume_XIV/The_Second_Ecumenical_Council/Historical_Excursus
notes: CAVEAT: the transmitted acts are disputed — some scholarship holds the Filioque in the Toledo III acts may be a later interpolation. Schaff argues the council itself had no suspicion it was using anything but the unaltered Constantinopolitan creed, and that 589 is the earliest date at which the words are found in the Creed. The milestone is therefore recorded with its verification record marked partially-verified. No passage is listed as invoked at the council, because no specific passage was verified as cited in the acts; do not pad passageIds. (D) The Filioque is a later formulation, not part of the biblical text or of the creed as adopted at Constantinople in 381. The Councils of Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), and Constantinople II (553) were checked as candidates in Era 3 and omitted: they are primarily Christological, and no direct bearing on the doctrine of the Trinity was established from a checked source in that pass. Coordinator note 2026-11-21: Era 3 and Era 4 independently researched this council under different ids (third-council-of-toledo-589 / council-of-toledo-589); the entries are merged here into one, keeping both verification records.

citation: The Canons of the Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, Canon 1 (Firmiter credimus) and Canon 2, Internet History Sourcebooks: Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University, https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/lateran4.asp (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: H. J. Schroeder, Disciplinary Decrees of the General Councils: Text, Translation and Commentary (St. Louis: B. Herder, 1937).

date.note: Fourth Lateran Council met in Rome, 11-30 November 1215, under Pope Innocent III; Canon 1 is the Firmiter credimus profession of faith.

notes: Canon 2 also condemns Abbot Joachim's tract against Peter Lombard and confesses with Lombard that there is one supreme entity which is truly Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, 'three persons and each one of them singly', so that in God there is only Trinity, not quaternity. Canon 2 quotes 1 John 5:7-8 (including the Johannine Comma) and John 10:29 and John 17:22 in the course of its argument; only 1john-5-7 is listed in passageIds, because it is the only one of the three that is in the 60-passage inventory (John 10:29 and John 17:22 are not). Coordinator correction 2026-11-21: thomas-aquinas removed from authorIds — Aquinas (born 1225) was not involved in the 1215 council; the link was an error in the era draft. The milestone's verification record does not assert his involvement.
summary: The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), in its first constitution Firmiter credimus, gave the classic medieval Latin profession of the Trinity: 'one true God, eternal and immense, omnipotent, unchangeable, incomprehensible, and ineffable, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; three Persons indeed but one essence, substance, or nature absolutely simple; the Father proceeding from no one, but the Son from the Father only, and the Holy Ghost equally from both, always without beginning and end.' (D) This is a thirteenth-century conciliar formulation — including the Latin 'equally from both' (filioque) — not a statement of any biblical text. Canon 2, against Joachim of Fiore, defended Peter Lombard's account of the one essence against the charge of quaternity.
title: Fourth Lateran Council (1215) — Firmiter credimus

citation: Council of Florence, Session 6, 6 July 1439, Laetentur Caeli (Decree of Union with the Greeks), trans. in the Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, as reproduced at Catholic Library, https://catholiclibrary.org/library/view?docId=/Magisterium-EN/XCT.285.html&chunk.id=00000065 (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Norman P. Tanner, ed., Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, vol. 1 (London: Sheed & Ward, 1990).

date.note: Laetentur Caeli was signed 5 July 1439 and promulgated 6 July 1439 at the Council of Florence (Session 6).

notes: The decree states that 'texts were produced from divine scriptures' in the debate, but the checked text names no specific biblical passage by reference, so no passage is listed in passageIds; do not pad. The union was rejected in the East and did not hold; Mark of Ephesus refused to sign. The decree's definition is recorded here as the Latin West's position, with the Eastern disagreement noted in the summary.
summary: The Council of Florence (1439), in the decree of union Laetentur Caeli, defined that 'the holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsistent being from the Father together with the Son, and proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration', and that the addition of 'and from the Son' (Filioque) to the creed was licitly and reasonably added. It also explained the Greek phrase 'through the Son' as meaning the Son is, like the Father, cause/principle of the Spirit's subsistence. (D) This is a fifteenth-century conciliar formulation of the filioque, not a statement of any biblical text; the Eastern churches rejected the union, and the disagreement is recorded, not harmonised.
title: Council of Florence (1439) — Laetentur Caeli on the Filioque
Augsburg Confession, Article I (Of God)

date.note: Presented to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530. Only the year is asserted here; the day and month (25 June) are not stated on the checked page.

summary: Article I confesses one divine essence in three coeternal persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - following the decree of the Council of Nicaea, and condemns the Manichaeans, Valentinians, Arians, Eunomians, Mohammedans, and the Samosatenes old and new. (D) This is a sixteenth-century confessional formulation; it restates the Nicene doctrine and must not be presented as the wording of the biblical texts themselves. Only Matthew 28:19 is listed, because it is the passage cited in the Article itself.
citation: Philip Melanchthon, The Augsburg Confession, in Triglot Concordia, trans. F. Bente and W. H. T. Dau (St. Louis: Concordia Publishing House, 1921), Article I. Edition: Triglot Concordia, trans. F. Bente and W. H. T. Dau (St. Louis: Concordia, 1921), pp. 37-95. URL: https://christian.net/pub/resources/text/wittenberg/concord/web/augs-001.html. Accessed 2026-11-20.

title: Racovian Catechism (first publication)

date.note: First published in Polish at Rakow, 1605 (Rees, Historical Introduction); Latin version 1609.

summary: The Catechism of the Polish Brethren, the first published statement of the Socinian position, argues that the joint naming of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19; 1 Cor. 12:4-6; 1 John 5:7) proves only their existence and their association in divine things, not three persons in one essence, and that the one God is the Father alone (1 Cor. 8:6). (D) A seventeenth-century dissenting publication; its position is recorded as the Catechism states it, without endorsement or refutation here. The three passages listed are the three testimonies the Catechism itself names together in Section III, Chapter 1.
citation: The Racovian Catechism, trans. Thomas Rees (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1818). Edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680. URL: https://archive.org/stream/racoviancatechi00reesgoog/racoviancatechi00reesgoog_djvu.txt. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: Dissenting milestone. Authorship is collective (Smalcius, Moskorzowski, Volkel; Socinus died 1604, before drafting), so authorIds is empty here; the associated author is recorded on the work record.

title: Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 2 (Of God, and of the Holy Trinity)

date.note: Completed and presented to both Houses of Parliament 4 December 1646 (Schaff, Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, section 94).

summary: Chapter 2 confesses one only living and true God, and that 'in the unity of the Godhead there be three Persons of one substance, power, and eternity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost' (II.3), with the Son eternally begotten of the Father and the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son. (D) A seventeenth-century confessional formulation; the listed passages are the proof texts printed with Chapter 2, not the formulation itself.
citation: The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), ch. 2. Edition: Text as in The Westminster Confession of Faith (CCEL, Creeds of Christendom); first printed December 1646. URL: http://www.ccel.org/creeds/westminster.htm. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: Corporate authorship: the Westminster Assembly; authorIds is empty. The passage list is exactly the Chapter 2 proof texts that fall within the 60-passage inventory: II.1 (Deut. 6:4; 1 Cor. 8:4, 6), II.2 (Rom. 9:5), II.3 (Matt. 3:16-17; 28:19; 2 Cor. 13:14; 1 John 5:7; John 15:26). John 1:14, 18 and Gal. 4:6 are also cited in II.3 but are not in the inventory, so they are not listed.
